claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about experimental design.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background that fear extinction mechanisms remain debated, with evidence for both inhibition and erasure mechanisms. Prior work suggests inhibition mechanisms are primarily studied using single-session extinction training, while erasure mechanisms have been studied with both single- and multiple-session protocols, leading to the hypothesis that different extinction protocols may engage different mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 provide a well-supported literature review establishing the scientific context. All claims are backed by appropriate citations to established work (C1-C9), and the inference that different mechanisms may be involved in different extinction protocols (C10) is a reasonable synthesis of the cited evidence.

results.result: IL neurons show transient CS-evoked excitatory activity during extinction recall after single-session extinction training (post-Ext1) in rats with successful extinction, but this activity disappears during subsequent extinction sessions (post-Ext2, post-Ext3). Rats with poor extinction recall show no significant IL activity changes throughout training.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are well-supported by behavioral data (C13), stable neuronal recordings from 72 neurons in 19 rats (C14), and appropriate statistical analyses (C15-C17: repeated measures ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.05). The conclusion (C18) logically follows from the data showing transient IL activity only after single-session extinction.

results.result: Ba neurons comprise distinct 'fear neurons' and 'extinction neurons' subpopulations. Fear neurons show CS-evoked activity after conditioning that disappears after extinction. Extinction neurons show CS-evoked activity only after single-session extinction training (post-Ext1), but this activity disappears after multiple-session extinction training.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 are supported by stable recordings from 130 Ba neurons in 27 rats (C20), appropriate statistical analyses (C22-C25: Friedman test with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.05), and consistency with prior literature (Herry et al., 2008). The conclusion that extinction neurons no longer reflect low fear state after multiple-session extinction (C26) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Ba-ITC synapses show transient potentiation after single-session extinction training, evidenced by reduced paired-pulse ratio and increased AMPA/NMDA ratio, but both pre- and post-synaptic enhancements return to baseline after multiple-session extinction training.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by electrophysiological measurements with appropriate statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. naïve; p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. naïve). The conclusion (C32) appropriately integrates both pre- and post-synaptic findings.

results.result: Inhibitory tone in LA principal neurons, measured by mIPSC amplitude, is decreased after fear conditioning and enhanced after single-session extinction training, but returns to baseline after multiple-session extinction training. mIPSC frequency also shows training-dependent changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.05). The data show significant changes in mIPSC amplitude consistent with prior work (Lin et al., 2009) and support the conclusion that local inhibition is no longer present after multiple-session extinction (C37).

results.result: Surface expression of β2 and γ2 GABAA receptor subunits in the LA increases after single-session extinction training but returns to baseline after multiple-session extinction training, while cadherin expression remains unchanged. These changes in GABAA receptor surface expression correlate with changes in inhibitory tone.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by biochemical data (surface biotinylation and Western blotting) with appropriate statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.05). The cadherin control (C41) strengthens the specificity of the findings. The conclusion (C42) reasonably links receptor expression changes to functional inhibitory tone changes.

results.result: T-LA synaptic efficacy is enhanced after fear conditioning and shows depotentiation after single-session extinction training that persists throughout multiple-session extinction training (post-Ext1, post-Ext2, post-Ext3), suggesting the erasure mechanism remains active across all extinction phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by input-output curve measurements with appropriate statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.005 for post-Cond vs. naïve; p<0.005 for post-Ext1 vs. post-Cond; p>0.05 among extinction groups). The conclusion (C48) that depotentiation persists throughout multiple-session extinction is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Cell-type specific ablation of ITC neurons using D-Sap significantly impairs extinction recall after single-session extinction training but has no effect after multiple-session extinction training, despite achieving comparable ITC neuron reduction in both conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by behavioral data and cell counts with appropriate statistical analyses (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.01 for behavioral impairment after single-session; p>0.05 after multiple-session; p<0.001 for ITC reduction in both cases). The dissociation between ITC lesion effects after single vs. multiple-session extinction strongly supports the conclusion (C52).

results.result: The main finding is that extinction mechanisms change when single-session extinction training is repeated: inhibition mechanisms (mediated by prefrontal cortex and ITC neurons) predominate during single-session extinction but subside after that, while erasure mechanisms (depotentiation at LA synapses) persist throughout multiple-session extinction training.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C65 represent the central conclusion integrating all experimental findings (Figures 1-7). The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: neuronal recordings (IL and Ba), electrophysiology (Ba-ITC synapses, LA inhibition, T-LA synapses), biochemistry (GABAA receptors), and lesion studies (ITC ablation). All component results show consistent patterns supporting this integrative model.

results.result: Summary of mechanistic dissociation: inhibition mechanism correlates (IL activity, Ba extinction neurons, Ba-ITC potentiation, LA inhibition, ITC requirement) disappear after multiple-session extinction, while erasure mechanism correlates (LA synaptic depotentiation and associated molecular markers) persist throughout extinction training.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 appropriately summarize the experimental findings from the current study (C60-C62) and integrate them with prior literature on molecular markers (C63-C64). The summary accurately reflects the data presented in Figures 1-7 and cited studies, providing a coherent synthesis of the mechanistic dissociation.

results.result: The coordinated disappearance of inhibition mechanisms across multiple brain regions (IL, Ba, LA, ITC) suggests the IL orchestrates these mechanisms via synaptic connections, and loss of IL responsiveness to CS after multiple-session extinction may drive the complete loss of inhibition mechanisms.
results.evaluation: While C66 accurately summarizes the coordinated disappearance observed in the data, and C67 is supported by citations to connectivity studies, the orchestration hypothesis (C68, C70) is speculative. C69 provides some supporting evidence (IL cells similar to Ba extinction neurons), but this is insufficient to definitively establish the proposed orchestration mechanism. The claims represent a reasonable hypothesis but require additional experimental validation (e.g., IL manipulation experiments during multiple-session extinction).

results.result: The functional interpretation proposes that inhibition mechanisms cope immediately and transiently with no-longer-fearful CSs, while erasure works persistently when CSs become habituated. The apparent contradiction with fear relapse after multiple-session extinction is addressed by distinguishing cellular erasure in the amygdala from brain-wide memory persistence or metaplastic reconstruction.
results.evaluation: C56 is a speculative functional interpretation of the findings. C57-C59 attempt to reconcile the erasure findings with known fear relapse phenomena, but these are largely speculative explanations. While C58 is supported by citations showing distributed fear memory traces, and C59 cites metaplasticity literature, neither explanation is directly tested in this study. These represent plausible hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: The study challenges the prevailing view that fear memory inhibition is the primary extinction mechanism, suggesting instead it represents a transient mechanism for early extinction. The IL may also play a role in triggering depotentiation at LA synapses during extinction training.
results.evaluation: C73 is a well-supported conclusion that challenges prevailing views based on the comprehensive experimental evidence. C74 is a speculative reinterpretation of IL function supported by citations to relevant connectivity and depotentiation studies (Likhtik et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2007). C75 provides additional support from recent literature (Do-Monte et al., 2015a). While C74 is speculative, it represents a reasonable hypothesis grounded in the data and literature.

results.result: The findings have translational implications: multiple-session extinction training in animals better models human exposure therapy, and human neuroimaging shows similar patterns (transient prefrontal enhancement, persistent amygdala reduction). This suggests targeting cellular changes after multiple-session extinction may yield more persistent therapeutic effects than targeting inhibition mechanisms.
results.evaluation: C76 makes a reasonable translational claim supported by citations to clinical literature. C77 provides supporting evidence from human neuroimaging (Quidé et al., 2012) showing parallel patterns. However, C78-C79 are speculative clinical implications that extend beyond the data. While the parallel between animal and human findings is intriguing, the therapeutic implications require direct clinical validation. The claims represent plausible translational hypotheses but are not definitively supported.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about neural circuits and mechanisms: IL function in extinction recall, Ba extinction neurons, amygdala circuitry (Ba-ITC-CeA), synaptic changes at Ba-ITC and LA synapses, and GABAA receptor involvement in LA inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C12, C19, C27-C29, C33, C38, C43-C44 appropriately cite established literature to provide context for the experimental work. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior studies. These background claims establish the foundation for the novel experimental findings.

results.result: Ba extinction neurons send inputs to IL neurons (inactivation impairs extinction), and Ba extinction neurons respond to CS with shorter latencies than IL extinction neurons, suggesting Ba may initiate the inhibition circuit.
results.evaluation: C71 is supported by citation to Senn et al., 2014. C72 is supported by data analysis referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 legend. Together, these claims provide evidence for an alternative hypothesis about circuit organization, though the authors acknowledge this remains speculative. The data support the latency difference, making this a valid observation.

results.result: The mechanisms underlying the disappearance of inhibition mechanisms during multiple-session extinction remain unclear and may involve erasure or a second round of inhibition, analogous to the debate about original fear extinction mechanisms.
results.evaluation: C80 is an appropriately cautious acknowledgment of the limits of the current study. The speculation is reasonable and draws a valid parallel to the original extinction debate. This represents an honest assessment of what remains unknown and suggests future research directions.

results.result: Methodological statements: all procedures were approved by institutional animal care committee, and all experiments were performed in a blinded fashion to avoid bias.
results.evaluation: C81-C82 are straightforward methodological statements about ethical approval and experimental design. These are important for assessing the rigor and ethical conduct of the research. The blinded design (C82) is particularly important for reducing bias in behavioral and histological assessments.
